|publisher=[[Bianet]]}}</ref>}}
}}
{{LGBT rights}}

Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer ([[LGBTQ]]) people in [[Turkey]] face significant challenges not experienced by non-LGBTQ residents. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the [[Ottoman Empire]] adopted a new penal code in 1858, and [[transgender]] people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988.<ref name="auto5">{{Cite web |last=Mahkemesi |first=Anayasa |title=Press Release Concerning the Decisions on the Rules Regarding Gender Reassignment {{!}} Anayasa Mahkemesi |url=https://www.anayasa.gov.tr/en/news/constitutionality-review/press-release-concerning-the-decisions-on-the-rules-regarding-gender-reassignment |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20260121163503/https://www.anayasa.gov.tr/en/news/constitutionality-review/press-release-concerning-the-decisions-on-the-rules-regarding-gender-reassignment |archive-date=2026-01-21 |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=www.anayasa.gov.tr |language=tr}}</ref> 

However, Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTQ are barred from serving openly in the military. Same sex relationships receive no legal recognition: same sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not available in Turkey, and same sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as joint parents.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Turkey - Rainbow Map |url=https://rainbowmap.ilga-europe.org/countries/turkey/ |access-date=2026-09-14 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Turkey (Türkiye) |url=https://www.state.gov/reports/2023-country-reports-on-human-rights-practices/turkey/ |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=United States Department of State |language=en-US}}</ref> 

When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, which made symbolic same sex weddings possible, though these carry no legal marital status.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":10" /><ref name=":15" /> Because Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorder in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, individuals who have legally changed their registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Turkish Civil Code: Volume I, Section I, Chapter II: Personal Status Registry |url=https://www.law.cornell.edu/gender-justice/resource/turkish_civil_code_volume_i_section_i_chapter_ii_personal_status_registry |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=LII / Legal Information Institute |language=en}}</ref><ref name="auto5"/>

[[Istanbul]] hosted the first gay pride march held in a [[Muslims|Muslim]] majority country in 2003, and annual marches in Istanbul, [[Ankara]] and other cities drew growing crowds through the 2010s, with the 2013 and 2014 Istanbul marches each attracting more than 100,000 participants.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-07-28 |title=Pride in Istanbul {{!}} Wilson Center |url=https://www.wilsoncenter.org/article/pride-istanbul |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=www.wilsoncenter.org |language=en}}</ref> Since 2015 however, authorities have banned [[Pride parade|Pride]] events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, and police have used [[tear gas]], [[Water cannon|water cannons]] and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-06-30 |title=Turkey: Pride march ban is a new low |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/eur44/1978/2015/en/ |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=Amnesty International |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Turkey |url=https://2021-2025.state.gov/reports/2017-country-reports-on-human-rights-practices/turkey/ |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=United States Department of State |language=en-US}}</ref>

In [[ILGA-Europe]]'s 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking, Turkey placed 47th out 49 countries assessed, ahead of only [[LGBTQ rights in Azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]] and [[LGBTQ rights in Russia|Russia]].<ref>{{Cite web |date= |title=Rainbow Map |url=https://rainbowmap.ilga-europe.org/ |access-date=2026-09-20 |website=[[ILGA-Europe]] |language=en-US}}</ref> In early 2026, Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to [[biological sex]]", though this provision was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. Public attitudes have shifted gradually, surveys by [[Kadir Has University]] found support for equal rights for LGBTQ people rising from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-11-08 |title=KHAS Institutional Research |url=https://www.khas.edu.tr/en/khas-institutional-research/ |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=Kadir Has University |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-11-08 |title=KHAS Kurumsal Araştırmalar |url=https://www.khas.edu.tr/khas-kurumsal-arastirmalar/ |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=Kadir Has Üniversitesi |language=tr-TR}}</ref> While a 2020 [[Pew Research Center]] survey found that 25% of the Turks believed homosexuality should be accepted by society, against 57% opposed.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Poushter |first=Jacob |last2=Kent |first2=Nicholas |date=2020-06-25 |title=The Global Divide on Homosexuality Persists |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2020/06/25/global-divide-on-homosexuality-persists/ |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=Pew Research Center |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2025 |title=Pew Research Center Spring 2019 Global Attitudes Survey June 25, 2020 Release |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/global/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2020/06/PG_2020.06.25_Global-Views-Homosexuality_TOPLINE.pdf}}</ref> In his 2023 winning speech, President [[Recep Tayyip Erdogan]] accused opposition parties of being pro-LGBTQ while labeling the LGBTQ+ community as "perverted movements".<ref name=":16">{{Cite web |last=Tzabiras |first=Marianna |date=2023-05-30 |title=LGBTQI+ groups address Erdoğan's victory speech |url=https://ifex.org/lgbtqi-groups-address-erdogans-victory-speech/ |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=IFEX |language=en-US}}</ref>

== History ==
[[File:XXI._Istanbul_Gay_Parade_Pride_-_Peace_Tower.jpg|250px|thumb|[[Istanbul Pride]] in 2013, [[İstiklal Avenue]], [[Istanbul]]]]
[[File:Gay_pride_Istanbul_2013_-_Taksim_Square.jpg|250px|thumb|[[Istanbul Pride]] in Taksim Square]]

=== During the Ottoman Empire ===
{{Main|Gender and sexual minorities in the Ottoman Empire}}
The [[Ottoman Turks|Ottomans]], before the 19th-century, did not base sexual identities on attraction to a specific gender but distinguished between active and passive partners, often distinguished as "the lover" and "the beloved".<ref name="aeon.co">{{Cite web |title=What Ottoman erotica teaches us about sexual pluralism {{!}} Aeon Ideas |url=https://aeon.co/ideas/what-ottoman-erotica-teaches-us-about-sexual-pluralism |access-date=2022-05-17 |website=Aeon |language=en}}</ref> Therefore, choice of a partner was merely based on taste and not on sexual identity. This made certain types of same-sex attraction permissible, but this attraction was most often legitimized in a [[Pederasty|pederastic]] context.<ref name="aeon.co" />

By the late 19th century, homosexual contact started to decline and the focus of desire turned to young girls. Ahmet Cevdet Pasha stated:<blockquote>Woman-lovers have increased in number, while boy-beloveds have decreased. It is as if the People of Lot have been swallowed by the earth. The love and affinity that were, in Istanbul, notoriously and customarily directed towards young men have now been redirected towards girls, in accordance with the state of nature.</blockquote>Research shows that the decline is in close relationship to the criminalization of homosexuality in the Western world, which followed repression of the queer community.<ref name="aeon.co" />

=== Republican period ===
{{Main|LGBT history in Turkey}}
In the 1980s, the national government, whether democratically elected or as a result of a coup d'état, opposed the existence of a visible LGBTQ community, especially within the political context.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}}

Some openly gay people were able to be successful in the 1980s. [[Murathan Mungan]] has been openly gay throughout his professional life as a successful poet and writer. However, many gay and bisexual men who lived during this period have since said in interviews that they felt pressured by social attitudes and government policy to remain in the closet about their sexual identity.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.qrd.org/qrd/www/world/europe/turkey/study.htm |title=Gay Identities |publisher=Qrd.org |access-date=2019-09-27}}</ref>
[[Image:Christopher_street_day_istanbul_1993.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Original T-shirt designed for the first Christopher Street Day celebration march in 1993]]

In the 1980s, the [[Radical Democratic Union|Radical Democratic Green Party]] expressed support for gay rights, including the work of a group of transgender people to protest police brutality. However, it was not until the 1990s that many members of the LGBTQ community in Turkey began to organise on behalf of their human rights.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}}

In 1993, [[Lambda Istanbul]] was created to campaign on behalf of LGBTQ rights in Turkey. In 1994, the [[Freedom and Solidarity Party]] banned discrimination on the basis of [[sexual orientation]] and [[gender identity]] within the party and nominated [[Demet Demir]], a leading voice of the community,<ref>{{Cite news
|url=http://www.sptimes.com/2003/01/17/Floridian/A_city_comes_out.shtml
|access-date=20 August 2008
|title=Floridian: A city comes out
|work=[[St. Petersburg Times]]
|date=17 January 2003
|first=Susan Taylor
|last=Martin|language=tr}}</ref> to successfully become the first transgender candidate for the local council elections in [[Istanbul]].

In 1993, organisers were denied permission to hold an LGBTQ pride parade. Similar opposition was expressed by the government in 1995 and 1996 for an LGBTQ film festival and academic conference. Government officials cited vaguely worded laws designed to protect public morality as justification for refusing to allow these public events to take place.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}}

In 1996, the [[Court of Cassation (Turkey)|Supreme Court]] overturned a lower court's ruling and removed a child from her lesbian mother on the grounds that homosexuality is "immoral".<ref>See [http://news.kaosgl.com/item/131 report of Kaos GL: Turkey's LGBT History: The 1990s] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090524022630/http://news.kaosgl.com/item/131 |date=24 May 2009 }}. Retrieved 16 October 2009.</ref>

Throughout the 1990s, reports by IHD, Turkey's Human Rights Association as well as international [[human rights organizations]] such as [[Amnesty International]] stated that transgender people were frequently harassed and beaten by police officers. One article even stated that police had set fire to an apartment block with many transgender people residing there.<ref>[The Guardian. "Turkey Turns on Its Decadent Past". Owen Bowcott, 1996]</ref>

Reports of harassment and violence against LGBTQ people still occur in the twenty-first century. In 2008, a gay Kurdish-Turk student, Ahmet Yıldız, was shot outside a café by his father and later died in the hospital.<ref name="taz.de">{{Cite news|url=https://www.taz.de/!5156656/|title=Ehrenmord in der Türkei: "Jeder soll wissen, ich bin schwul"|first=Deniz|last=Yücel|date=7 September 2009|via=www.taz.de|newspaper=Die Tageszeitung: Taz}}</ref><ref name="report with details on the killing">The German Democratic Turkey Forum (DTF) has prepared a [http://www.tuerkeiforum.net/enw/index.php/The_killing_of_Ahmet_Y%C4%B1ld%C4%B1z_%282008%29 report with details on the killing] and the subsequent court case; accessed on 31 March 2011.</ref> Sociologists have called this Turkey's first publicised gay [[honour killing]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/11/26/world/europe/26turkey.html|title=Soul-Searching in Turkey After a Gay Man Is Killed|last=Bilefsky|first=Dan|date=26 November 2009|work=New York Times |pages=A16 |access-date=26 November 2009}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/europe/was-ahmet-yildiz-the-victim-of-turkeys-first-gay-honour-killing-871822.html|title=Was Ahmet Yildiz the victim of Turkey's first gay honor killing?|author=Nicholas Birch|work=The Independent |access-date=27 September 2008 | location=London | date=19 July 2008}}</ref> The wish of the Turkish Government to join the [[European Union]] has put some pressure on the government to grant official recognition to LGBTQ rights. The report on progress in Turkey for the accession to the European Union of 14 October 2009, the European Commission for Enlargement wrote:<ref name="EU2009">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=TURKEY 2009 PROGRESS REPORT|url=https://ec.europa.eu/neighbourhood-enlargement/sites/near/files/pdf/key_documents/2009/tr_rapport_2009_en.pdf|access-date=2021-01-18|website=}}</ref>
:The legal framework is not adequately aligned with the EU acquis...
:[[Homophobia]] has resulted in cases of physical and sexual violence. The killing of several transsexuals and transvestites is a worrying development. Courts have applied the principle of 'unjust provocation' in favour of perpetrators of crimes against transsexuals and transvestites.

In 2003, Turkey became the first Muslim-majority country in which a gay pride march was held.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://pride.yahoo.com/2010/ |title=Yahoo |access-date=2010-06-28 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120213161714/http://pride.yahoo.com/2010/ |archive-date=13 February 2012 }}</ref> In Istanbul (since 2003) and in [[Ankara]] (since 2008) gay marches were being held each year with an increasing numbers of participation until 2015.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2023/06/turkiye-istanbul-pride-showdown-highlights-threat-to-lgbti-rights/#:~:text=Istanbul%20Pride%20has%20been%20celebrated,the%20police%20and%20arbitrary%20detention. | title=Türkiye: Istanbul Pride showdown highlights threat to LGBTI rights | date=23 June 2023 }}</ref> 

On 30 June 2013, [[Istanbul Pride]] parade attracted almost 100,000 people.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.telegraaf.nl/tv/21696299/__Gay_Pride_in_Istanbul_groot_succes__.html|title=Gay Pride in Istanbul groot succes|work=telegraaf.nl|access-date=23 August 2015|archive-date=28 July 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170728210152/http://www.telegraaf.nl/tv/21696299/__Gay_Pride_in_Istanbul_groot_succes__.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> The protesters were joined by [[Gezi Park]] protesters, making the 2013 Istanbul Pride the biggest pride event ever held in Turkey.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://dunya.milliyet.com.tr/taksim-deki-onur-yuruyusu-ne-bbc/dunya/detay/1730407/default.htm|title=Taksim'deki Onur Yürüyüşü'ne BBC yorumu: Bugüne kadar... – Milliyet Haber|date=1 July 2013|access-date=23 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131104131320/http://dunya.milliyet.com.tr/taksim-deki-onur-yuruyusu-ne-bbc/dunya/detay/1730407/default.htm|archive-date=4 November 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> The 2014 Istanbul pride attracted more than 100,000 people. The 2015, 2016, 2017, and 2018 pride parades were banned by local authorities, and participants were faced with police attacks. In June 2013, the first [[İzmir Pride]] took place with 2,000 participants.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kaosgl.com/sayfa.php?id=14410|title=İzmir'de İlk Onur Yürüyüşünde Sokaklar Doldu Taştı|access-date=23 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141110125712/http://www.kaosgl.com/sayfa.php?id=14410|archive-date=10 November 2014|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref> On 3 June 2018, the 6th İzmir Pride Parade peacefully took place with over 50,000 participants.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://hornet.com/stories/pride-parade-in-istanbul-two/|title=It Does Turkish LGBTQ+ People No Favors to Pretend Turkey Is a Homophobic Nightmare|first=Hornet|last=Networks|date=8 July 2018|website=Hornet}}</ref> Another pride took place in [[Antalya]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.siyahpembe.org/index.php/antalya-ve-izmir-onur-haftasini-yuruyusle-selamlayacak/ |title=Antalya ve İzmir, Onur Haftası'nı Yürüyüşle Selamlayacak |work=Siyah Pembe Üçgen İzmir |access-date=23 August 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130701210325/http://www.siyahpembe.org/index.php/antalya-ve-izmir-onur-haftasini-yuruyusle-selamlayacak/ |archive-date=1 July 2013 }}</ref> Politicians from the main opposition party, [[Republican People's Party|CHP]] and another opposition party, [[Peace and Democracy Party|BDP]] also lent their support to the demonstration.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ntvmsnbc.com/id/25227029/|title=İstiklal Caddesi 10 bin renk!|date=27 June 2011|work=NTV|access-date=23 August 2015}}</ref> The pride march in Istanbul does not receive any support of the municipality or the government.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/n.php?n=istanbul-becoming-proud-of-pride-week-2011-06-19|title=ARTS-CULTURE – Istanbul becoming proud of Pride Week|access-date=23 August 2015|archive-date=3 September 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110903051211/http://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/n.php?n=istanbul-becoming-proud-of-pride-week-2011-06-19|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.vocativ.com/09-2013/over-the-rainbow-hopes-dim-for-turkeys-once-promising-gay-revolution/ |title=Gay rights in Turkey face uphill battle<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=19 September 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131111212406/http://www.vocativ.com/09-2013/over-the-rainbow-hopes-dim-for-turkeys-once-promising-gay-revolution/ |archive-date=11 November 2013 |url-status=dead |df=dmy-all }}</ref>

In 2009, amateur football referee [[Halil İbrahim Dinçdağ]] came out as gay and was subsequently banned from refereeing football matches. In December 2015, the [[Turkish Football Federation]] was ordered to pay 23,000 lira in compensation for dismissing Dinçdağ.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-35194359|title=Gay referee wins Turkey court case|date=29 December 2015|work=BBC News}}</ref>

On 21 September 2011, the Minister of Family and Social Policies [[Fatma Şahin]] met with an LGBTQ organisation. She said that the government will actively work together with LGBTQ organisations. She submitted a proposal for the acceptance of LGBTQ individuals in the new constitution that Parliament planned to draft in the coming year. She was calling on Members of Parliament to handle the proposal positively. She asserted that "if freedom and equality is for everybody, then sexual orientation discrimination should be eliminated and the rights of these [[LGBTQ]] citizens should be recognised."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.todayszaman.com/news-257544-lgbt-gains-recognition-from-government-for-first-time.html |title=LGBT gains recognition from government for first time<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=22 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150521205138/http://www.todayszaman.com/news-257544-lgbt-gains-recognition-from-government-for-first-time.html |archive-date=21 May 2015 |url-status=dead |df=dmy-all }}</ref>

On 9 January 2012, a columnist named Serdar Arseven for an [[Islamism|Islamist]] newspaper called ''[[Yeni Akit]]'' wrote an article calling LGBTQ people perverts. The [[Court of Cassation (Turkey)|Court of Cassation]] penalised Yeni Akit with 4,000 [[Turkish lira|TL]] fine and Serdar Arseven with 2,000 TL for hate speech.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kaosgl.com/sayfa.php?id=10321|title=Biz Üskül'ü Eleştirdik Davayı Kaos GL Açtı!|access-date=23 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812213414/http://www.kaosgl.com/sayfa.php?id=10321|archive-date=12 August 2014|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

In May 2012, the BDP requested the writers of the new Turkish constitution to include [[same-sex marriage]] in that constitution. It was rejected by the biggest party in the Turkish Parliament, the [[AK Party|AKP]], and an opposition party, [[Nationalist Movement Party|MHP]], while supported by the main opposition party, the [[Republican People's Party|CHP]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.haber10.com/haber/279069/|title=Haber 10 – BDP'nin eşcinsel evlilik isteği tartışılıyor|access-date=23 August 2015|archive-date=30 June 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120630100958/http://www.haber10.com/haber/279069/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.timeturk.com/tr/2012/05/15/bdp-nin-escinsel-evlilik-istegi-tartisiliyor.html|title=BDP'nin eşcinsel evlilik isteği tartışılıyor|access-date=23 August 2015|archive-date=8 December 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208074512/http://www.timeturk.com/tr/2012/05/15/bdp-nin-escinsel-evlilik-istegi-tartisiliyor.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

On 29 May 2013, a parliamentary research motion regarding LGBTQ rights in Turkey was proposed and discussed in the [[Grand National Assembly of Turkey|parliament of Turkey]]. Despite support from pro-Kurdish BDP, secularist CHP, and the abstention of Turkish nationalist party MHP, the motion was rejected by votes of the ruling party AKP. AKP MP Türkan Dağoğlu cited the scientific articles on homosexuality published in the US in 1974 and said, "Homosexuality is an abnormality. Same-sex marriages may not be allowed. It would cause social deterioration." For the research motion, CHP MP Binnaz Toprak said, "In the 1970s there were scientists suggesting that black people were not as smart as white people in the US. Hence the science of today doesn't accept the findings of those times. Your sayings can not be allowed."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ntvmsnbc.com/id/25446001|title=Tension in Parliament over LGBT Rights|publisher=Ntvmsnbc|date= 29 May 2013|access-date=29 May 2013|language=tr}}</ref>

LGBT-themed DVDs can also be legally sold in Turkey, albeit DVDs with sexually explicit content may only be sold to people eighteen years of age or older. In 2013, a Turkish vendor was charged with selling "immoral" DVDs because the DVD movies featured gay sexually explicit content. Judge Mahmut Erdemli from the court in Istanbul overturned the criminal charges. He ruled that gay sex is natural, stated that an individual's sexual orientation should be respected, and cited examples of same-sex marriages in Europe and in the Americas.<ref name="lgbtqnation.com">{{cite web|url=http://www.lgbtqnation.com/2013/02/turkish-court-says-gay-sex-is-natural-in-ruling-against-pornography-vendor/|title=Turkish Court says gay sex is natural in ruling against pornography vendor|work=LGBTQ Nation|access-date=23 August 2015|date=2013-02-20}}</ref>

In 2013, Grindr, a social networking and hookup app targeted to gay men, was banned by the Istanbul Anatolia 14th Criminal Court of Peace.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Cutler |first=Tess |date=2015-02-11 |title=Meet Joel Simkhai, the Israeli foundr of Grindr |url=https://jewishjournal.com/cover_story/161967/ |access-date=2026-05-10 |website=Jewish Journal |language=en-US}}</ref> 

On 12 August 2013, the Constitutional Reconciliation Commission, which was drafting a new constitution of the Republic and was composed of four major parliamentary parties including [[Peace and Democracy Party|Kurds]], [[Republican People's Party|secularists]], [[Justice and Development Party (Turkey)|Islamists]] and [[Nationalist Movement Party|nationalists]], agreed to provide constitutional protection against discrimination for LGBTQ individuals.<ref name="eşitlik">{{Cite news|url=http://t24.com.tr/haber/anayasa-komisyonu-lgbt-haklarinda-uzlasti/236767|access-date=13 August 2013|title=LGBT hakları, 'eşitlik' maddesinin gerekçesinde yer alacak|work=t24|date=12 August 2013|language=tr|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131211113046/http://t24.com.tr/haber/anayasa-komisyonu-lgbt-haklarinda-uzlasti/236767|archive-date=11 December 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> The draft was later cancelled.<ref name="fadeofhopes">{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-turkey-constitution-idUSBRE9AH0OV20131118|access-date=7 December 2013|title=Hopes fade for a new Turkish constitution|work=Reuters|date=18 November 2013}}</ref>

On 17 July 2014, [[Court of Cassation (Turkey)|Turkey's Supreme Court]] ruled that referring to gays as "perverted" constitutes hate speech.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://lgbtinewsturkey.com/2014/07/17/constitutional-court-decision-on-hate-speech-sexual-orientation|title=CONSTITUTIONAL COURT OF TURKEY: REFERRING TO GAYS AS PERVERTS IS HATE SPEECH|work=LGBTI NEWS TURKEY|date=17 July 2014|access-date=18 July 2014|archive-date=23 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190523225001/https://lgbtinewsturkey.com/2014/07/17/constitutional-court-decision-on-hate-speech-sexual-orientation/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In November 2016, Turkey, along with Georgia, Israel, Japan, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, South Korea, Sri Lanka, Thailand, East Timor and Vietnam, were the only [[Asia]]n countries in the [[United Nations]] to vote in favor of the appointment of an independent expert to raise awareness of the discrimination faced by the LGBTQ community and to find ways to properly protect them.<ref>[https://76crimes.com/2016/11/21/anti-lgbti-push-at-u-n-falls-short/ Anti-LGBTI push at U.N. falls short] Erasing 76 Crimes</ref>

In June 2018, the embassy of Turkey, along with ambassadors from 51 countries signed an open letter of support for LGBTQ rights in Poland.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Turkey among signatories of open letter supporting LGBT rights in legally-restrictive Poland - Turkey News|url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkey-among-signatories-of-open-letter-supporting-lgbt-rights-in-legally-restrictive-poland-133059|access-date=2021-06-29|website=Hürriyet Daily News|date=10 June 2018 |language=en}}</ref>

In March 2021, Turkey [[Istanbul Convention#Denunciation of convention by Turkey|withdrew]] from the [[Istanbul Convention]], blaming the LGBT community for its withdrawal. In an official statement by the Turkish Presidency, it argued that "the Istanbul Convention, originally intended to promote women's rights, was hijacked by a group of people attempting to normalize homosexuality – which is incompatible with Turkey's social and family values." The view was shared by conservative Turkish ruling party [[Justice and Development Party (Turkey)|Justice and Development Party]] (AKP), who claim that the agreement promotes homosexuality.<ref name="ReasonOfWithdrawal">{{cite web| url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/biden-calls-turkeys-exit-from-treaty-for-women-unwarranted-turkey-joe-biden-recep-tayyip-erdogan-istanbul-white-house-b1820290.html | title=Biden calls Turkey's exit from treaty for women unwarranted | publisher=Independent | date=21 March 2021 | access-date=21 March 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210321183529/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/biden-calls-turkeys-exit-from-treaty-for-women-unwarranted-turkey-joe-biden-recep-tayyip-erdogan-istanbul-white-house-b1820290.html | archive-date=21 March 2021 | url-status=live }}</ref> Turkish President [[Recep Tayyip Erdoğan]] justified their withdrawal as "completely legal."<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|title=Erdoğan insists it's at his discretion to pull Turkey out of İstanbul Convention|url=https://www.bianet.org/english/women/241444-erdogan-insists-it-s-at-his-discretion-to-pull-turkey-out-of-istanbul-convention|access-date=2021-03-27|website=Bianet - Bagimsiz Iletisim Agi|archive-date=20 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210720154110/https://bianet.org/english/women/241444-erdogan-insists-it-s-at-his-discretion-to-pull-turkey-out-of-istanbul-convention|url-status=live}}</ref> Later in 2021 restrictions and political rhetoric targeting LGBTQ people intensified. Amnesty International reported that Turkish authorities imposed blanket bans on and other restrictions on Pride marches and used unnecessary, and in some cases, excessive force against participants. Anti-LGBTQ rhetoric from senior government officials also increased during the period surrounding the 2023 elections.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-05-17 |title=Türkiye: Discriminatory restrictions and violence against Pride protesters must not be repeated |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/05/turkiye-discriminatory-restrictions-and-violence-against-pride-protesters-must-not-be-repeated/ |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=Amnesty International |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-06-23 |title=Türkiye: Istanbul Pride showdown highlights threat to LGBTI rights |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2023/06/turkiye-istanbul-pride-showdown-highlights-threat-to-lgbti-rights/ |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=Amnesty International |language=en}}</ref>

Following the 2023 presidential election, LGBTQ rights remained a main issue in Turkish politic rhetoric. After winning re-election in May 2023 President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan accused opposition parties of being "pro-LGBTQ" and referred to LGBTQ people as part of "perverted movement" in his victory speech. LGBTQ organizations [[17 Mayıs]] and [[Kaos GL]] condemned the rhetoric and said that the election campaign had been marked by hostility towards LGBTQ people. The organizations also pledged to continue their advocacy of LGBTQ equality and freedom.<ref name=":16" /><ref>{{Cite web |title='Our struggle is bigger than his words': LGBTI+ groups react to Erdoğan's victory speech |url=https://bianet.org/haber/our-struggle-is-bigger-than-his-words-lgbti-groups-react-to-erdogan-s-victory-speech-279514 |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=bianet.org |language=en}}</ref>

Restrictions continued in 2024 and 2025. Pride events and LGBTQ themed gatherings were repeatedly disallowed, while police detained participants and activists. Amnesty International reported that the 2024 Pride season was marked by bans on gatherings and violence against protestors.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024 |title=TÜRKİYE: ACTIVISTS REMAIN DEFIANT DESPITE CHILLING EFFECT OF UNLAWFUL BANS OF PRIDES |url=https://www.amnesty.org/es/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/EUR4487602024ENGLISH.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-06-12 |title=Türkiye: Prides must be allowed to proceed |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/eur44/9489/2025/en/ |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=Amnesty International |language=en}}</ref>

In May 2025, Erdogan declared a "Decade of Family and Population" beginning in 2026, with a focus on promoting traditional family structures and improving the country's birth rate. During his speech, Erdogan attacked the LGBTQ movement as a "threat" to "not only the family but also women, children, and human dignity", explaining that these "perversions" were "legitimized under the guise of respect for personal choices" and had "turned into a tyranny that tolerates no differing opinion, a full-fledged fascism". He stated that "the fight against LGBT perversion is also a fight for freedom, dignity, and the future of humanity." <ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-07-27 |title=Türkiye adopts 10-year vision to track population trends, strengthen family policies |url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkiye-adopts-10-year-vision-to-track-population-trends-strengthen-family-policies-224850 |access-date=2026-09-16 |website=Hürriyet Daily News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Erdogan launches 'Decade of Family and Population' from 2026 to 2035 |url=https://www.trtworld.com/article/0e0fbe85c91e |access-date=2026-09-16 |website=TRT World |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-05-27 |title=Erdoğan targeted LGBTI+ individuals at the International Family Forum and declared the 2026-2035 period as the “Decade of Family and Population” |url=https://kaosgl.org/en/single-news/erdogan-targeted-lgbti-individuals-at-the-international-family-forum-and-declared-the-2026-2035-period-as-the-decade-of-family-and-population |access-date=2026-09-16 |website=[[Kaos GL]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Hubbard |first=Ben |last2=Timur |first2=Safak |date=2026-05-17 |title=Erdogan Wants Turkey to Have More Babies. Few Parents Are Listening. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/17/world/europe/erdogan-turkey-demography-babies-family-planning-economy.html |access-date=2026-09-16 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

Authorities began to increasingly use [[obscenity]] laws to target LGBTQ organisations, arguing that pro-LGBTQ materials violated [[public morality]]. In April 2026, Genç LGBTI+ was ordered to dissolve after posting materials on social media that officials in [[İzmir]] considered "obscene" and in violation of the Turkish constitution's article on protecting the family. Eleven founders of the group were also put on trial.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Genç LGBTİ+ Derneği “müstehcenlik” iddiasıyla kapatıldı |url=https://bianet.org/haber/genc-lgbti-dernegi-mustehcenlik-iddiasiyla-kapatildi-314467 |access-date=2026-09-16 |website=bianet.org |language=tr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-04-08 |title=Turkey puts 11 leaders of LGBTQ+ association on trial for 'obscenity' |url=https://www.euronews.com/2026/04/08/turkey-puts-11-leaders-of-lgbtq-rights-association-on-trial-for-obscenity |access-date=2026-09-16 |website=euronews |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Gärtner |first=Katja |date=2026-04-07 |title=Joint Statement: Alarming escalation in repression of LGBTI+ activists and organisations in Türkiye |url=https://www.ilga-europe.org/news/joint-statement-alarming-escalation-in-repression-of-lgbti-activists-and-organisations-in-turkey/ |access-date=2026-09-16 |publisher=ILGA-Europe |language=en-GB}}</ref> Obscenity is not clearly defined in law.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How Turkey’s vague obscenity law is becoming a tool to criminalize LGBTI+ visibility |url=https://bianet.org/haber/how-turkeys-vague-obscenity-law-is-becoming-a-tool-to-criminalize-lgbti-visibility-323560 |access-date=2026-09-18 |website=bianet.org |language=en}}</ref> In September 2026, in support of the Decade of Family and Population, Turkish authorities began a crackdown on LGBTQ+ and HIV support organizations known as "My Family is Safe". On 14 September 2026, [[12 September Turkish LGBTQ raids|authorities began coordinated raids]] in several cities, arresting dozens of people and blocking the groups' websites. According to reports the investigation involves 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses. Officials say the crackdown is intended to protect children, families and public order, and have raised allegations involving foreign funding and criminal activity.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-09-13 |title=Turkish police detain dozens in raids on gay bars and homes of LGBTQ+ activists |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cpve191wy47o |access-date=2026-09-16 |website=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Buyuk |first=Hamdi Firat |date=2026-09-16 |title=Turkey Stages Wide-Ranging LGBT Crackdown for 'Family Safety' |url=https://balkaninsight.com/2026/09/16/turkey-stages-wide-ranging-lgbt-crackdown-for-family-safety/bi/ |access-date=2026-09-16 |website=Balkan Insight |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Kiper |first1=Cinar |title=Turkish authorities launch crackdown on LGBTQ+ and HIV support groups |url=https://apnews.com/article/turkey-lgbtq-hiv-crackdown-c782f5318613126fe072d29133e6bf5d |website=Associated Press News |access-date=19 September 2026 |date=13 September 2026}}</ref> The [[European Union]] called out the crackdown and stated that "stigmatization and discrimination are contrary to the values of the union".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Ünveren |first1=Burak |title=Turkey's rights groups, EU call out LGBTQ+ crackdown |url=https://www.dw.com/en/turkeys-rights-groups-eu-call-out-lgbtq-crackdown/a-79284021 |website=dw.com |access-date=19 September 2026 |date=15 September 2026}}</ref>

==Laws and litigation==
Turkey is in the [[European Convention on Human Rights|ECHR]], which has [[case law]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ks.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr-ks/guide_lgbti_rights_eng|title=Guide on the case-law of the European Convention on Human Rights}}</ref> The [[wikisource:Constitution_of_the_Republic_of_Turkey_(2017)#B._Right_to_hold_meetings_and_demonstration_marches|constitution]] says that everyone has the right to march peacefully.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lawyers investigated for monitoring Pride march in Aydın |url=https://bianet.org/haber/lawyers-investigated-for-monitoring-pride-march-in-aydin-321150 |access-date=2026-07-30 |website=bianet.org |language=en}}</ref> KAOS GL has a case pending since 2023,<ref>{{Cite web |title=KAOS GEY VE LEZBIYEN KÜLTÜREL ARAŞTIRMALAR VE DAYANIŞMA (KAOS GL) DERNEĞI contre la Türkiye |url=https://hudoc.echr.coe.int/#%7B%22languageisocode%22:%5B%22FRE%22%5D,%22appno%22:%5B%225797/22%22,%2227507/23%22%5D,%22documentcollectionid2%22:%5B%22COMMUNICATEDCASES%22%5D,%22itemid%22:%5B%22001-234812%22%5D%7D |access-date=2026-07-30 |website=hudoc.echr.coe.int}}</ref> alleging ineffective remedies in [[Judicial system of Turkey|Turkish law]] against alleged discrimination such as bans on some Pride marches.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-16 |title=Debate Over a New Judicial Package in Türkiye Heightens the Urgency of Kaos GL v. Türkiye Before the ECtHR |url=https://opiniojuris.org/2026/01/16/debate-over-a-new-judicial-package-in-turkiye-heightens-the-urgency-of-kaos-gl-v-turkiye-before-the-ecthr/ |access-date=2026-07-30 |website=Opinio Juris |language=en-US}}</ref> According to a February 2026 report by [[Türkiye (newspaper)|''Türkiye'' newspaper]] the government is considering a introducing a law criminalizing publicly encouraging "behavior contrary to biological sex", with a sentence of one to three years in prison.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gazetesi |first=Türkiye |date=2026-02-17 |title=LGBT'yi övene 3 yıl hapis yolda! Sapkın akımlara karşı ağır yaptırımlar geliyor |url=https://www.turkiyegazetesi.com.tr/gundem/lgbtyi-ovene-3-yil-hapis-yolda-sapkin-akimlara-karsi-agir-yaptirimlar-yolda-1771320 |access-date=2026-07-30 |website=Türkiye Gazetesi |language=tr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Report: Government revives draft bill criminalizing LGBTI+s |url=https://bianet.org/haber/report-government-revives-draft-bill-criminalizing-lgbti-s-316850 |access-date=2026-07-30 |website=bianet.org |publisher=[[Bianet]] |language=en}}</ref> However, this was not in the 2026 [[omnibus bill]] (the 12th judicial package).<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":10">{{Cite web |date=23 June 2026 |title=12th Judicial Reform Package: Provisions on LGBTI+ people, social media identity verification, child penalties, and alimony removed from the bill |url=https://bianet.org/haber/12-yargi-paketi-lgbti-lar-sosyal-medyada-kimlik-dogrulama-cocuk-cezalari-ve-nafaka-tekliften-cikarildi-320786 |access-date=30 July 2026 |website=Bianet |language=tr}}</ref><ref name=":11">{{Cite web |title=Has the 12th Judicial Reform Package of 2026 been published in the Official Gazette? When will the 12th Judicial Reform Package be published? |url=https://www.hurriyet.com.tr/bilgi/galeri/12-yargi-paketi-2026-resmi-gazetede-yayimlandi-mi-12-yeni-yargi-paketi-ne-zaman-resmi-gazetede-yayimlanacak-43256254 |access-date=30 July 2026 |website=Hürriyet |language=tr}}</ref>[[File:İzmir_Gay_Pride_2014.jpg|thumb|Pride in [[İzmir]] in 2014]]
Gay sex between consenting adults in private is not a crime in Turkey. Turkey does not recognise [[same-sex marriages]], [[civil unions]] or domestic partnership benefits. Same-sex marriage or civil unions are not illegal, but they are officially impossible, as the law does not recognize official same-sex marriage. However, when the 12th judicial package was passing through parliament, provisions that discriminated against LGBTQ individuals were removed; this made symbolic same-sex weddings and marriages possible.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":11" />

Under Turkish law, marriage is still defined as a union between a man and a woman. Therefore, the gender listed in official records is the determining factor. A trans woman officially registered as female can marry someone officially registered as male., A trans man officially registered as male can marry someone officially registered as female. In other words, what matters legally is not whether a person is trans, but the gender recorded in the civil registry. LGBT marriage other than for trans individuals is legally impossible.<ref name=":12">{{cite web|access-date=3 August 2026 |publisher=Nüfus ve Vatandaşlık İşleri Genel Müdürlüğü |title=Evlenme İşlemleri |url=https://nvi.gov.tr/evlenme-islemleri}}<!-- auto-translated from Turkish by Module:CS1 translator --></ref><ref name=":13">{{cite web|access-date=3 August 2026 |publisher=Anayasa Mahkemesi |title=Cinsiyet Değişikliği Hakkındaki Kurallara İlişkin Kararın Basın Duyurusu |url=https://www.anayasa.gov.tr/tr/haberler/norm-denetimi-basin-duyurulari/cinsiyet-degisikligi-hakkindaki-kurallara-iliskin-kararlarin-basin-duyurusu/}}<!-- auto-translated from Turkish by Module:CS1 translator --></ref><ref name=":14">{{cite web|access-date=3 August 2026 |publisher=Anayasa Mahkemesi |title=Cinsiyet Değişikliğine İzin Verilmesini Düzenleyen Kurala İlişkin Karar |url=https://www.anayasa.gov.tr/tr/haberler/norm-denetimi-basin-duyurulari/cinsiyet-degisikligine-izin-verilmesini-duzenleyen-kurala-iliskin-itiraz-basvurusu-hakkinda-karar}}<!-- auto-translated from Turkish by Module:CS1 translator --></ref>

==Military service==
{{See also|Pink certificate}}

In Turkey, [[Conscription in Turkey|compulsory military service]] applies to all male Turkish citizens between the ages of 18 and 41. However, the Turkish military openly discriminates against homosexuals by barring them from serving in the military. At the same time, Turkey – in violation of its obligations under the [[European Convention on Human Rights]] – withholds any recognition of [[conscientious objection]] to military service.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wri-irg.org/news/alerts/msg00110.html |title=TURKEY: Conscientious objector Mehmet Bal beaten in prison &#124; War Resisters' International |publisher=Wri-irg.org |access-date=20 January 2011}}</ref> Some objectors must instead identify themselves as "sick" – and some were forced to undergo what [[Human Rights Watch]] calls "humiliating and degrading" examinations to "prove" their homosexuality.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hrw.org/english/docs/2008/05/22/turkey18900.htm |title=Turkey: Homophobic Violence Points to Rights Crisis &#124; Human Rights Watch |publisher=Hrw.org |date=21 May 2008 |access-date=20 January 2011}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/magazine-17474967 |title=Proving you're gay to the Turkish army |work=BBC News |date=26 March 2012 |access-date=18 May 2013|last1=Azizlerli |first1=Emre }}</ref>

In October 2009 the report of the EU Commission on Enlargement stated: "The Turkish armed forces have a health regulation which defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness and identifies homosexuals as unfit for military service. Conscripts who declare their homosexuality have to provide photographic proof. A small number have had to undergo humiliating medical examinations."<ref name="EU2009" />

In November 2015, the Turkish Armed Forces removed the clause stating that a draftee must "prove" their homosexuality. Draftees may decide to disclose their sexuality verbally and receive an 'unfit report' during their medical examination which exempts them from service, or must not disclose their orientation in any form for a year if a military doctor agrees to grant them a 'fit report' and serve their conscription. Those who disclose their homosexuality and receive an 'unfit report' may be subject to future discrimination in public life as the military's record of homosexuals in the drafting process has resulted in several cases of public leaks.<ref name="Gurcan 2015">{{cite web |url=http://www.al-monitor.com/pulse/originals/2015/11/turkey-military-gay-rights-homosexual-picture.html |title=Gays seeking military exemption in Turkey no longer need to provide visual proof of their homosexuality |access-date=20 November 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171024154055/http://www.al-monitor.com/pulse/originals/2015/11/turkey-military-gay-rights-homosexual-picture.html |archive-date=24 October 2017 |url-status=dead |df=dmy-all |date=2015-11-17 }}</ref> Homosexuality remains grounds for expulsion for commissioned officers, non-commissioned officers and military students under the Turkish Armed Forces Discipline Law.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.resmigazete.gov.tr/eskiler/2013/02/20130216-1.htm|title=Başbakanlık Mevzuatı Geliştirme ve Yayın Genel Müdürlüğü|website=www.resmigazete.gov.tr}}</ref>

There is little support in the army in favour of greater acceptance; in a 2015 study asking 1,300 officers "whether homosexuals should be allowed to serve in the army", 96.3% answered negatively.<ref name="Gurcan 2015" />

==Discrimination protections==
[[File:Bulent_Ersoy.jpg|thumb|left|[[Bülent Ersoy]], the first openly transgender celebrity (singer) starts wearing makeup and feminine clothing in her performances and makes appearances on Turkish National TV (TRT) during the 1970s.]]
[[File:Zeki Müren cropped.jpg|left|thumb|A statue of [[Zeki Müren]], one of the prominent figures of the [[Ottoman classical music|Turkish classical music]] who never commented on his [[sexual orientation]], but the general public opinion was that he was [[homosexual]]]]

Although discrimination is officially prohibited,<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> the [[European Commissioner for Enlargement|EU Commission on Enlargement]] has for some time recommended that Turkey improves its laws and their implementation to properly protect LGBTQ people,<ref name=":15">{{Cite web |title=Türkiye Report 2025 - Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood |url=https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/turkiye-report-2025_en |access-date=2026-08-22 |website=enlargement.ec.europa.eu |language=en}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=5}} but as of 2025 Turkey had not done so and in their annual report the commission wrote that "The legal protection of the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer(LGBTIQ) persons is insufficient and not aligned with the EU acquis. Moreover, LGBTIQ persons are subject to discrimination, hate speech and stigmatisation." and that authorities were "granting official permissions for demonstrations that promote exclusion and discrimination".<ref name=":15" />{{Reference page|page=40}}

In 2011, Öykü Evren Özen, a transgender woman from the northwestern province of [[Bursa]], became a candidate for deputy from the main opposition party, [[Republican People's Party]], or CHP. She was the first transgender lawmaker of Turkey during the general elections.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/transsexual-activist-candidate-to-main-oppositions-list-for-bursa-municipal-assembly.aspx?pageID=238&nID=56155&NewsCatID=341|title=Transsexual activist candidate to main opposition's list for Bursa – POLITICS|access-date=12 October 2013}}</ref>

The main opposition, CHP, proposed gay rights to the Turkish parliament on 14 February 2013.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/gay-rights-proposed-to-turkish-parliament.aspx?pageID=238&nID=41174&NewsCatID=338|title=Gay rights proposed to Turkish Parliament – POLITICS|date=15 February 2013 |access-date=23 August 2015}}</ref>

Lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) individuals are among the most [[social vulnerability|vulnerable]] [[asylum seeker]]s and refugees in Turkey today.<ref>[http://www.hyd.org.tr/staticfiles/files/unsafe_haven_report.pdf Unsafe Haven: The Security Challenges Facing Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual and Transgender Asylum Seekers and Refugees in Turkey] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111005013401/http://www.hyd.org.tr/staticfiles/files/unsafe_haven_report.pdf|date=5 October 2011}}, a joint publication of Helsinki Citizens' Assembly – Turkey and [[ORAM (organization)|ORAM]] – Organization for Refuge, Asylum & Migration, June 2009</ref> Their access to rights and services is limited in Turkey as a result of anti-LGBTQ sentiments of state actors and the general public.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Koçak |first=Mert |date=2020-01-02 |title=Who is "Queerer" and Deserves Resettlement?: Queer Asylum Seekers and Their Deservingness of Refugee Status in Turkey |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/19436149.2020.1704506 |journal=Middle East Critique |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=29–46 |doi=10.1080/19436149.2020.1704506 |s2cid=213611770 |issn=1943-6149|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In August 2013, three major political parties in the parliament including the secularist [[Republican People's Party|CHP]] which worked with [[Peace and Democracy Party|BDP]] on the matter, conservative [[Peace and Democracy Party (Turkey)|AKP]] and nationalist [[Nationalist Movement Party|MHP]], has agreed to provide constitutional protection against discrimination for LGBTQ people.<ref name="eşitlik"/> The draft was later canceled due to nonconcurrences regarding other subjects in the new constitutional draft.<ref name="fadeofhopes"/>

Can Çavuşoğlu, a Turkish activist, has launched a campaign as the first openly gay mayoral candidate of [[Turkey]], Çavuşoğlu announced a bid to run in the Black Sea region, a town of Bulancak, [[Giresun]], home to about 60,000, in the March 2014 local elections.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.globalpost.com/dispatch/news/regions/europe/turkey/130914/can-cavusoglu-wants-be-turkeys-first-openly-gay-mayor|title=Can Cavusoglu wants to be Turkey's first openly gay mayor|publisher=globalpost|access-date=14 September 2013}}</ref>

In February 2015, the main opposition CHP introduced a bill to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in both public and private sectors. The bill seeks equal recruitment, pay, promotion, dismissal in the workplace and reforms in the [[Turkish Armed Forces]] Code of Discipline that would allow members of the military to serve openly.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kaosgl.com/page.php?id=18860|title=Turkey's main opposition proposed labor bill for LGBT people|access-date=23 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150819213701/http://www.kaosgl.com/page.php?id=18860|archive-date=19 August 2015|url-status=dead|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

In 2015, the Kurdish [[Peoples' Democratic Party (Turkey)|Peoples' Democratic Party]] publicly announced that they will have LGBTQ and feminist candidates. [[Barış Sulu]], a candidate of the left-wing People's Democratic Party (HDP), became the first openly gay man to run for the Turkish parliament.<ref>{{cite news|title=Meet The Pro-Gay, Pro-Women Party Shaking Up Turkish Politics|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2015/06/08/turkey-hdp-party_n_7537648.html|access-date=12 May 2016|work=The Huffington Post|date=8 June 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Turkey now has its first ever gay parliamentary candidate|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/first-ever-openly-gay-parliamentary-candidate-stands-for-election-in-turkey-10274746.html|access-date=12 May 2016|work=The Independent|date=25 May 2015|language=en-GB}}</ref>

In January 2019, the 34th Labor Court in Istanbul issued the first verdict in a legal case surrounding three garbage truck drivers in the Kağıthâne Municipality who were fired by their employer after it was alleged that they were in a gay relationship with a 27-year-old garbage collector. The garbage collector, identified only as M.Ş., had told the authorities that he had engaged in sexual relationship "from time to time" with the three truck drivers. The drivers, aged between 43 and 51, had sued the municipality and its subcontractor in April 2018, citing what they described as unjust termination of their contract. On 29 January, the court ruled in favor of one of the plaintiffs, identified as R.S., concluding that his contract was unjustly terminated. His attorney had told the court that the plaintiff "had got nothing to do with that incident," while the company lawyers had claimed that his dismissal was part of "rightful termination" due to the sexual relationship at work. If the ruling is approved in the appeals process too, the subcontractor will be forced to return the plaintiff to his previous job or to compensate him. A hearing for one of the other two cases, which still continue, was held in February.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ahvalnews.com/lgbti-rights/turkish-man-sacked-gay-relationship-wins-legal-battle|title=Turkish man sacked for gay relationship wins legal battle|website=Ahval|access-date=10 February 2019|archive-date=12 February 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190212011414/https://ahvalnews.com/lgbti-rights/turkish-man-sacked-gay-relationship-wins-legal-battle|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkish-court-issues-first-verdict-in-gay-garbage-men-case-140871|title=Turkish court issues first verdict in 'gay garbage men case' - Turkey News|website=Hürriyet Daily News|date=30 January 2019 }}</ref>

==Gender identity and expression==
In Turkey, the minimum age required to get sex reassignment surgery is 18. In order for one to change one's gender section on an identity card, the procedure must be conducted at a state hospital. Sex reassignment surgery is available in Turkey's major cities like [[Istanbul]], Ankara, İzmir and Antalya.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.duvarenglish.com/health-2/2020/01/20/a-heavy-price-to-pay-for-sex-change-in-turkey#:~:text=Filiz%20Gazi%2F%20DUVAR-,In%20Turkey%2C%20the%20minimum%20age%20required%20to%20get%20sex%20reassignment,%2C%20Ankara%2C%20Izmir%20and%20Antalya.|title = The heavy price to pay for a sex change in Turkey| date= 20 January 2020}}</ref> However, Turkey has very limited trans rights compared to other countries that allow gender reassignment. Hormone replacement therapy for transgender individuals is not covered by the government healthcare system, and there is no direct discrimination protection regarding gender identity in Turkish law.<ref>{{Citation |title=Situation report on discriminations against women in Turkey |url=https://euromedrights.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/factsheet-Turkey_EN-2.pdf |publisher=[[EuroMed Rights]] |access-date=2025-06-15}}</ref>

==Media regulations==
{{Main|LGBTQ in Turkish media}}

In 2013, Grindr, a social networking and hookup app targeted to gay men, was banned by the Istanbul Anatolia 14th Criminal Court of Peace.<ref name=":1" />

Under article 8/1f of Turkish broadcasting law, the [[Radio and Television Supreme Council]] (RTÜK) has the authority to suspend or ban television programmes that are contrary to "national and moral values" or "the principle of protection of family", and issue fines of up to 3% of an outlet's annual revenue for violations of broadcasting law. In 2019, legislation extended RTÜK's scope to include internet "broadcasters" as well. RTÜK has been regularly accused of using vague rulings under article 8/1f to target independent and opposition-run broadcasters.<ref name=":17" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-12-15 |title=Turkey: Crackdown on Independent TV Channels |url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2020/12/15/turkey-crackdown-independent-tv-channels |access-date=2026-09-17 |website=Human Rights Watch |language=en}}</ref> RTÜK president Ebubekir Sahin has stated that the regulator's goal is "protecting children, youth and the family structure."<ref name=":17">{{Cite web |last=Buyuk |first=Hamdi Firat |date=2025-12-31 |title=Turkish Media Regulator Embraces New Role: Stifling Dissent |url=https://balkaninsight.com/2025/12/31/turkish-media-regulator-embraces-new-role-stifling-dissent/bi/ |access-date=2026-09-17 |website=Balkan Insight |language=en-US}}</ref> 

RTÜK has used article 8/1f to target pro-LGBT content; in 2023, [[Halk TV]] was charged with contravening "national and moral values" after trans activist [[Esmeray Özadikti]] said on-air "I am sure that LGBT+ children, especially those from [[Generation Z]], who are seeing me on the screen right now, are very happy and do not feel alone."<ref>{{cite news |title=RTÜK'ten "Kızıl Goncalar" dizisine üst sınırdan ceza |url=https://www.aa.com.tr/tr/gundem/rtukten-kizil-goncalar-dizisine-ust-sinirdan-ceza/3094518 |work=www.aa.com.tr |language=tr}}</ref> In 2025, these efforts intensified after the regulator signed a "protocol" with the Istanbul Family Foundation to promote pro-family content in broadcasting, stating that it would "combat" LGBTQ+ content in broadcasting as a violation of "national and moral values".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-08-13 |title=RTÜK'ten 4 dijital platforma ceza |url=https://www.dha.com.tr/gundem/rtukten-4-dijital-platforma-ceza-2926593 |access-date=2026-09-17 |website=DHA {{!}} Demirören Haber Ajansı |language=tr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Minute |first=Turkish |date=2025-03-07 |title=Turkish broadcasting watchdog declares 2025 ‘Year of Combatting LGBTQ+ Content’ |url=https://turkishminute.com/2025/03/07/turkish-broadcast-watchdog-declares-2025-year-of-combatting-lgbtq-content2/ |access-date=2026-09-17 |website=Turkish Minute |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-08-03 |title=Turkish media watchdog signs 'pro-family protocol' with Istanbul Family Foundation |url=https://www.duvarenglish.com/turkish-media-watchdog-signs-pro-family-protocol-with-istanbul-family-foundation-news-65772 |access-date=2026-09-17 |website=Duvar English |language=tr-TR}}</ref> In September 2025, it issued fines against [[Amazon Prime Video]], [[Disney+]], [[HBO Max]], [[Netflix]], and [[Mubi (streaming service)|Mubi]], totalling 3% of their domestic revenue, for hosting LGBTQ+ content it deemed a violation of moral and family values.<ref>{{cite news |title=RTÜK fines streaming platforms, orders removal of films over 'anti-family' content|url=https://bianet.org/haber/rtuk-fines-streaming-platforms-orders-removal-of-films-over-anti-family-content-311665|work=Bianet|date=18 September 2025|access-date=27 May 2026}}</ref> 

==Restriction of expression==
The rights of expression regarding LGBT topics have been eroded alongside the [[democratic backsliding in Turkey]] since 2013.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Esena |first1=Berk |last2=Gumuscu |first2=Sebnem |year=2016|title=Rising competitive authoritarianism in Turkey |journal=[[Third World Quarterly]] |volume=37|issue=9|pages=1581–1606|doi=10.1080/01436597.2015.1135732 |hdl=11693/36632 |s2cid=155983134 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

In Turkey, everyone has the constitutionally protected right to hold a peaceful protest without prior permission, and may only be restricted on the grounds of national security, public order, prevention of commission of crime, protection of public health and public morals, and to protect the rights of others.<ref>{{cite act |type=article |index=34 |date=16 April 2017 |legislature=Turkish Grand National Assembly |title=Türkiye Cumhuriyeti Anayasası |trans-title=The Constitution of the Republic of Turkey |url=https://www.tbmm.gov.tr/develop/owa/tc_anayasasi.maddeler?p3=34 |language=Turkish}}</ref> According to its organisers, the [[Istanbul Pride]] parade in 2015 was denied permission on account with the Muslim holy month of [[Ramadan]]. After it was held regardless, police dispersed the attendees with a water cannon.<ref name="WC">{{cite news |url=http://in.reuters.com/article/turkey-rights-gay-pride-idINKCN0P80O420150628 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307102335/http://in.reuters.com/article/turkey-rights-gay-pride-idINKCN0P80O420150628 |url-status=dead |archive-date=March 7, 2016 |title=Turkish police use water cannon to disperse gay pride parade - by Mehmet, Caliskan and Yesmin Dikmen|date=28 June 2015 |agency=in.reuters.com |access-date=26 December 2025}}</ref> In 2016, it was banned again and arrests were made as participants tried to hold the rally regardless of the prohibition.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aljazeera.com/news/2017/06/istanbul-lgbt-march-banned-security-concerns-170624181917813.html|title=Istanbul LGBT march banned over 'security concerns'|website=www.aljazeera.com|access-date=2017-11-20}}</ref> It was banned again in 2017, and in 2018 it was banned again and arrests were made as participants tried to hold the rally regardless of the prohibition. It was banned again in 2019. In 2020, due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], it was held online with no official interference.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://prideistanbul.org/ |website= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201201060914/http://prideistanbul.org/ |title=28. İstanbul LGBTİ+ Onur Haftası ve 18. Onur Yürüyüşü Basın Açıklaması |trans-title=Press Release Regarding the 28th Istanbul LGBTI+ Pride Week and the 18th Pride Parade |archive-date=1 December 2020 |access-date=1 December 2020 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2017, the capital city of Ankara banned the public showing of films and exhibitions related to LGBT issues. The governor's office claimed the action was taken to provide peace and security. It stated that such exhibitions could cause different groups of society to "publicly harbour hatred and hostility" towards each other.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://uk.reuters.com/article/uk-turkey-lgbt/turkish-capital-bans-lgbt-cinema-exhibitions-idUKKBN1DJ0BS|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171119125957/https://uk.reuters.com/article/uk-turkey-lgbt/turkish-capital-bans-lgbt-cinema-exhibitions-idUKKBN1DJ0BS|url-status=dead|archive-date=19 November 2017|title=Turkish capital bans LGBT cinema, exhibitions|date=19 November 2017|work=Reuters}}</ref> As of 2025 the [[Pink Life QueerFest]] is still banned.<ref name=":15" />{{Reference page|page=40}}

In November 2017, the Ankara governor's office under state of emergency imposed an indefinite ban on LGBTI-focused public events. The emergency rule ended in July 2018, but the ban has not lifted.<ref name="HRW2"/>

In June 2018, the Governorship of [[Adana]] banned local Adana pride parade.<ref>{{Cite web |date=8 July 2018 |title=Turkey's governor's office in Adana province bans LGBTI pride march |url=https://stockholmcf.org/turkeys-governors-office-in-adana-province-bans-lgbti-pride-march/ |access-date=2018-07-08 |website=stockholmcf.org}}</ref> In October 2018, the government extended the ban to LGBTI-focused events generally without giving any idea about the end date.<ref name="HRW2">{{cite web|url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2019/02/14/turkey-end-ankara-ban-lgbti-events |title=Turkey: End Ankara Ban on LGBTI Events|access-date=14 February 2019|publisher=Human Rights Watch|date=14 February 2019}}</ref> In May 2019, police in Ankara broke up a student Pride march at the [[Middle East Technical University]], arresting at least 25 students.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gaystarnews.com/article/police-violent-student-pride-march-turkey/|title=Police violently break up student Pride march in Turkey|date=10 May 2019|website=Gay Star News|access-date=5 June 2019|archive-date=7 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201107232042/https://www.gaystarnews.com/article/police-violent-student-pride-march-turkey/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2019/05/turkey-appalling-violence-used-against-students-holding-pride-march/|title=A Pride march in Ankara has been violently broken up by police|website=www.amnesty.org|date=10 May 2019}}</ref>

On 14 June 2019, the 7th İzmir Pride, the 3rd Antalya Pride and the 27th Istanbul pride were banned by the cities' governors.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bianet.org/haber/izmir-lgbti-pride-week-and-antalya-pride-week-banned-209412|title=İzmir LGBTI+ Pride Week and Antalya Pride Week Banned|website=bianet.org}}</ref><ref name="m.bianet.org">{{Cite web|url=https://bianet.org/haber/on-what-grounds-is-pride-parade-not-permitted-209765|title=‘On What Grounds is Pride Parade not Permitted?’|website=bianet.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bianet.org/haber/governor-of-istanbul-rejects-pride-march-application-209473|title=Governor of İstanbul Rejects Pride March Application|website=bianet.org}}</ref> On 19 June, a court suspended said ban.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bianet.org/haber/love-wins-court-suspends-izmir-pride-week-ban-209530|title='Love Wins': Court Suspends İzmir Pride Week Ban|website=bianet.org}}</ref> On 22 June 2025, Turkish police dispersed a crowd gathered in [[İzmir]] for a public press statement by the 7th Izmir LGBT+ Pride Week Organizing Committee regarding the governorate's pride parade ban. After allowing the statement to be read, police detained 17 people.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ahvalnews.com/turkey-lgbti/17-detained-during-press-statement-over-pride-ban-turkeys-izmir|title=17 detained during press statement over Pride ban in Turkey's İzmir|website=Ahval|language=en|access-date=2019-06-28|archive-date=3 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210703045707/https://ahvalnews.com/turkey-lgbti/17-detained-during-press-statement-over-pride-ban-turkeys-izmir|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://sendika63.org/2019/06/7-izmir-lgbti-onur-yuruyusune-polis-saldirisi-17-gozalti-552183/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190624190632/http://sendika63.org/2019/06/7-izmir-lgbti-onur-yuruyusune-polis-saldirisi-17-gozalti-552183/|url-status=usurped|archive-date=24 June 2019|title=7. İzmir LGBTİ+ Onur Yürüyüşü'ne polis saldırısı: 17 gözaltı|website=Sendika.Org|language=tr|access-date=2019-06-28}}</ref>

On 25 June 2019, the Governorship of Mersin banned all LGBTQ events to be held in the province for 20 days under the Turkish Law on Meetings and Demonstrations "with the aim of maintaining public well-being and public peace, preventing crimes and protecting public health, public morality and safety of life and property of citizens." The ban went in effect in the 5th Mersin Pride Week, which was to be held between 1–7 July.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bianet.org/haber/lgbti-events-banned-in-mersin-209813|title=LGBTI+ Events Banned in Mersin|website=bianet.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gazeteduvar.com.tr/turkiye/2019/06/26/mersinde-onur-haftasi-yasagi/|title=Mersin'de Onur Haftası yasağı|website=www.gazeteduvar.com.tr|date=26 June 2019|language=tr|access-date=2019-07-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://ahvalnews.com/lgbti/turkeys-southern-province-mersin-bans-pride-march|title=Turkey's southern province of Mersin bans Pride March|website=Ahval|language=en|access-date=2019-07-17|archive-date=14 July 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190714203050/https://ahvalnews.com/lgbti/turkeys-southern-province-mersin-bans-pride-march|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.diken.com.tr/mersinde-onur-haftasi-etkinlikleri-genel-ahlak-gerekcesiyle-yasaklandi/|title=Mersin'de Onur Haftası etkinlikleri 'genel ahlak' gerekçesiyle yasaklandı|date=2019-06-26|website=Diken|language=en-US|access-date=2019-07-17}}</ref>
In June 2021, police blocked the first [[Eskişehir]] pride parade.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.duvarenglish.com/turkish-police-attack-eskisehirs-first-planned-pride-march-detain-20-news-58016|title=Turkish police attack Eskişehir's first planned Pride march, detain 20|website=duvarenglish.com|date=7 January 2021 |access-date=2021-07-01}}</ref>

==Public opinion==
According to a survey conducted by the [[Kadir Has University]] in Istanbul in 2016, 33 percent of people said that LGBTQ people should have equal rights. This increased to 45 percent in 2020. Another survey by Kadir Has University in 2018 found that 55.3 percent of people would not want a homosexual neighbour. This decreased to 46.5 percent in 2019.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Nearly Half of People Think LGBTI+s Should Have Equal Rights|url=https://bianet.org/english/lgbti/221831-survey-nearly-half-of-people-think-lgbti-s-should-have-equal-rights|access-date=13 February 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Public Perceptions of Gender Roles and the Status of Women in Turkey|url=https://gender.khas.edu.tr/en/survey-public-perceptions-gender-roles-and-status-women-turkey|access-date=13 February 2022}}</ref>

Attitudes towards the legalization of same-sex unions in Turkey are mixed. A 2015 poll by [[Ipsos]] found that 27% of the Turkish public was in favor of legalizing same-sex marriage, while 19% preferred civil unions instead.<ref name="Ipsos 2015">{{cite web|url=http://www.ipsos-na.com/news-polls/pressrelease.aspx?id=6866|title=Of 23 Countries Surveyed, Majority (65%) in 20 Countries Support Legal Recognition of Same-Sex Unions|date=March 29, 2015|publisher=Ipsos|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150603194659/http://www.ipsos-na.com/news-polls/pressrelease.aspx?id=6866|archive-date=2015-06-03}}</ref> 25% of those surveyed were against any form of legal recognition for same-sex couples and 29% stated that they did not know which option to choose.<ref name="Ipsos 2015"/>
